paragraphs: Federated learning must often proceed with whichever clients are currently available. Limited connectivity and computing resources mean that only a subset contributes in any round. This paper studies how those participation patterns affect convergence, addressing a gap between analyses based on idealized availability and more general analyses that retain a nonzero optimality error.

The authors introduce a generalized version of federated averaging that amplifies parameter updates at intervals spanning multiple rounds. Their analysis gathers the effect of client participation into a single mathematical term. This gives them a common framework for examining different participation patterns instead of treating every availability scenario as an unrelated problem.

Analyzing that term produces convergence upper bounds for a range of stochastic and non-stochastic participation patterns. In specific settings, the bounds match either a stochastic gradient descent lower bound or existing leading results. The contribution is therefore a unified way to connect participation to convergence, accompanied by practical insights and experiments, rather than a claim that every participation pattern performs equally well.
neurips-2022-a-unified-analysis-of-feder.tldr: A generalized federated averaging method and unified analysis connect varied client participation patterns to convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: Pre-trained language models face two connected practical problems: their size makes them expensive, and reliance on dataset biases can hurt performance when the data distribution changes. Earlier evidence that sparse subnetworks retain performance largely concerned in-distribution evaluation. This paper asks whether removing parameters can also coexist with robustness to dataset bias.

The authors study BERT on three natural language understanding tasks. They examine subnetworks found after fine-tuning, subnetworks extracted before being fine-tuned separately, and subnetworks obtained without parameter fine-tuning. Across these scenarios and different training and compression methods, their experiments consistently find subnetworks that combine sparsity with robustness.

The paper also uses out-of-distribution information to explore the potential performance of these subnetworks, finding sparse BERT subnetworks described as almost unbiased. That finding is tied to an investigation using such information. Further analysis examines how to search more efficiently, and the authors propose a way to improve performance at high sparsity. Together, the results support pursuing efficiency and robustness jointly in the studied BERT settings.
neurips-2022-a-win-win-deal-towards-spar.tldr: Experiments with BERT find sparse subnetworks that also resist dataset bias across three extraction and fine-tuning scenarios.

paragraphs: This paper studies a bandit problem in which agents occupy a graph and each agent plays a stochastic bilinear game with its neighbors. The graph makes the learning problem depend on interactions between agents. Choosing actions also creates a combinatorial optimization problem that is NP-hard, preventing direct use of existing regret-based linear or bilinear bandit algorithms.

The authors propose what they identify as the first regret-based algorithm for this setting. It follows optimism in the face of uncertainty: the method uses uncertainty about outcomes when deciding which actions look promising. This principle supplies a learning strategy for a setting where the graph creates an additional computational obstacle.

Their theoretical guarantee bounds alpha-regret by a quantity growing roughly as the square root of the number of rounds, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Because the guarantee concerns alpha-regret, its approximation qualification matters when interpreting the result. The analysis also shows that graph structure affects convergence, and experiments support the approach. The contribution combines a new algorithm with an account of how network interactions shape learning.
neurips-2022-an-alpha-no-regret-algorith.tldr: An optimistic algorithm achieves a roughly square-root alpha-regret bound for bilinear bandit games played across a graph.

paragraphs: Visual correspondence means identifying how image content matches across frames. It is central to many animation applications, but evaluating it requires examples that capture the complexity of animated scenes. The authors argue that existing cartoon correspondence datasets have overly simple compositions and repetitive motion, making them inadequate stand-ins for real animation.

AnimeRun addresses this by converting open-source 3D movies into complete scenes rendered in a 2D style. The resulting data include moving backgrounds alongside interactions among multiple subjects. These choices make correspondence involve several simultaneous sources of motion, rather than only an isolated subject moving through a simple scene.

The authors report dataset statistics showing closer resemblance to real anime in image composition and richer motion than existing datasets. They also evaluate several optical flow and segment matching methods, establishing a benchmark and examining their shortcomings on animation. The contribution is both a dataset and an evaluation setting: it provides more demanding animation examples and evidence about how existing correspondence methods handle them.
neurips-2022-animerun-2d-animation-visua.tldr: AnimeRun turns open-source 3D movies into a 2D animation correspondence dataset with complex scenes and motion.

paragraphs: The Wasserstein-2 distance compares distributions through an optimal transport problem. Gaussian smoothing modifies that comparison by adding noise to both distributions before measuring their distance. This paper asks how closely the smoothed distance approximates the original one when the distributions are discrete and the amount of added noise is small.

The authors derive precise approximation bounds and identify a change in behavior across a critical noise threshold. Their stated result assumes that the optimal transport plan is unique and forms a perfect matching. Under that condition, the difference between the original and smoothed distances scales exponentially in the inverse squared noise level below the threshold, and linearly with noise above it.

This distinction matters because reducing noise can improve approximation at very different rates in the two regimes. Below the threshold, sufficiently small noise yields exponentially close agreement with the unsmoothed distance. The result explains a strong approximation property of Gaussian-smoothed transport while tying it to the stated structure of the optimal matching, rather than asserting the same behavior for every pair of distributions.
neurips-2022-asymptotics-of-smoothed-was.tldr: Under a unique perfect-matching transport plan, sufficiently small Gaussian noise gives exponentially accurate Wasserstein-distance approximations.

paragraphs: Researchers compare neural networks by measuring similarities between their internal representations. This paper identifies a problem with two widely used measures, RSA and CKA: relationships already present among the input examples can influence the similarity score. As a result, the score can suggest functional agreement that does not accurately reflect how the networks behave.

The authors describe consequences including spuriously high similarity between completely random networks and inconsistent relationships between domains in transfer learning. They propose adjusting for input-space population structure using covariate adjustment regression. The correction aims to make comparisons more informative about network function while preserving the original measures' intuitive invariance properties.

Their results show improved resolution when identifying functionally similar networks across domains. In applications, adjusted CKA agrees more consistently with domain similarity in transfer learning and correlates more strongly with similarity in out-of-distribution accuracy. The findings support treating input structure as a confounder when interpreting representation comparisons, and provide a generally applicable correction to existing measures rather than requiring an entirely different comparison framework.
neurips-2022-deconfounded-representation.tldr: Adjusting RSA and CKA for input-data structure makes neural-network similarity measurements more informative about functional behavior.

paragraphs: Randomized smoothing can certify that a model's prediction remains unchanged throughout a bounded neighborhood of an input. Existing certificates are optimal when restricted to the class scores at that input. This paper asks whether information from surrounding locations can enlarge the certified region without contradicting that restricted optimality result.

The proposed approach combines the transitivity of certifications with the geometry of input space. It considers a set of certified regions and measures the smallest distance to points on their boundary. Using relationships among those regions provides local information beyond the class scores at the single input being tested.

On Tiny-Imagenet, the approach improves certifications for more than 80% of instances and yields an average increase of 5% in the associated certification. The authors also report a uniform four-percentage-point increase in achieved certified radius when combining the technique with training processes that enhance the radius. These findings show that certificates optimal under one information restriction can still improve when additional geometric information is available.
neurips-2022-double-bubble-toil-and-trou.tldr: Combining nearby certificates through geometry and transitivity improves randomized-smoothing robustness guarantees beyond single-input score information.

paragraphs: Markdown pricing requires a seller to learn demand while only lowering, never raising, the price. This creates an irreversible aspect to exploration: a price reduction constrains later choices. The paper models this as a continuum bandit problem with a non-increasing action sequence and the goal of maximizing expected revenue over a finite horizon.

Under broad assumptions of unimodality and Lipschitz continuity, earlier results give regret of order T to the three-quarter power for markdown pricing, versus T to the two-thirds power without the constraint. The authors ask how that comparison changes when demand belongs to a specified parametric family, such as a linear or exponential family.

They introduce markdown dimension, a measure of the complexity of a parametric demand family, and establish tight regret bounds within this framework. These bounds resolve their questions about improved learning rates and the difficulty added by monotonicity under the framework's assumptions. The central insight is that the structure of the demand family matters when assessing the cost of learning with irreversible price reductions.
neurips-2022-dynamic-pricing-with-monoto.tldr: Markdown dimension characterizes tight learning guarantees for dynamic pricing when prices can only decrease and demand is parametric.

paragraphs: Simulation-based Bayesian inference estimates model parameters from observations when explicit likelihood evaluation is unavailable. Many workflows summarize observations using scientifically meaningful features. This paper addresses how to determine which features actually reduce uncertainty about parameters, rather than treating every supplied summary statistic as equally informative.

A straightforward comparison would infer parameters with and without each feature, but repeated posterior estimation becomes expensive for large or nested feature sets. The authors instead build on neural likelihood estimation. They show that a trained surrogate likelihood can be marginalized after training, allowing selected features to be integrated out before the posterior is inferred.

This reuse of the trained likelihood provides a more efficient route to assessing feature contributions. The authors demonstrate it by identifying informative features for parameter inference in an example Hodgkin-Huxley neuron model using electrophysiological observations. The contribution connects feature importance to posterior uncertainty and is presented as applicable beyond neuroscience to simulation-based inference workflows that rely on data features.
neurips-2022-efficient-identification-of.tldr: Marginalizing a trained neural likelihood enables more efficient assessment of which features reduce uncertainty in simulation-based inference.

paragraphs: Privileged information is extra information available during training but absent when a model makes predictions in use. It can be valuable when training examples are scarce. This paper studies intermediate time-series observations as privileged information, asking how they can improve learning for nonlinear prediction problems involving underlying latent dynamics.

Earlier work established an expectation-based advantage in linear-Gaussian dynamical systems over unbiased classical learners. The authors revisit that analysis and extend theoretical guarantees to nonlinear tasks when the mapping between latent variables and observations is known up to a linear transformation. This condition defines the setting covered by their theoretical extension.

For cases where that mapping is unknown, they propose algorithms based on random features and representation learning. Empirical results support the theoretical findings and demonstrate the potential of privileged time-series information for nonlinear prediction. The work therefore separates a setting with a stated structural guarantee from a more general setting explored algorithmically, while pursuing the same goal of extracting more training value from limited examples.
neurips-2022-efficient-learning-of-nonli.tldr: Training-only time-series information can improve nonlinear prediction, with theoretical guarantees under a specified latent-observation mapping condition.

paragraphs: Deep learning applied to echocardiograms could support identifying heart structures, estimating cardiac function, and predicting clinical outcomes. A major obstacle is the limited availability of large, carefully annotated training datasets. Useful pre-trained visual representations could help models adapt to new tasks or settings with fewer labeled examples.

This paper introduces a suite of benchmarks for pre-training and evaluating echocardiographic representations using publicly accessible datasets. Its unified evaluation protocol, ETAB, measures how well a representation generalizes to common downstream tasks. The focus is on transferable visual features and their usefulness across clinically relevant tasks, rather than evaluating a representation solely within its original training setting.

The authors use the framework to evaluate leading vision-modeling pipelines. Its contribution is a shared, accessible basis for comparing representation learning approaches in echocardiography. By standardizing the evaluation question and protocol, ETAB is intended to encourage further research and progress toward cardiovascular applications; the abstract presents that broader impact as an aspiration, rather than an established clinical outcome.
neurips-2022-etab-a-benchmark-suite-for-.tldr: ETAB standardizes evaluation of how well pre-trained echocardiographic representations transfer to clinically relevant tasks.

paragraphs: Many fairness methods assume access to demographic labels during training, but privacy or legal concerns can make those labels unavailable. Existing approaches without demographics often use Rawlsian max-min objectives. The authors argue that these constraints can be too strict for improving group fairness and can substantially reduce predictive accuracy.

The paper proposes knowledge distillation as an alternative. An overfitted teacher model supplies soft labels, which express graded predictions rather than only a single assigned class. Preliminary experiments suggest that training with these labels can benefit fairness. The authors also analyze the method theoretically and interpret its effect as reweighting examples according to errors.

Experiments on three datasets show improvements over the compared state-of-the-art alternatives, with notable gains in group fairness and relatively small accuracy decreases. This evidence supports soft-label distillation as a useful approach in the studied settings where demographic information is absent from training. The reported outcome retains an accuracy tradeoff, while offering a different way to influence fairness through the training targets.
neurips-2022-fairness-without-demographi.tldr: Distillation from an overfitted teacher improves group fairness without training-time demographics in experiments, with relatively small accuracy losses.

paragraphs: Pipeline-parallel training splits a model across machines, making communication of intermediate activations a potential bottleneck on slow networks. This paper introduces AQ-SGD to compress that communication. Its central choice is to compress changes in activations instead of directly compressing the activation values themselves.

That design supports a convergence rate of O(1/√T) for non-convex objectives under activation compression. The analysis avoids assumptions of gradient unbiasedness that do not hold for deep models with nonlinear activation functions. The authors also show that the method can be implemented efficiently without adding end-to-end runtime overhead.

In language-model fine-tuning experiments with up to 1.5 billion parameters, AQ-SGD uses 2–4-bit activation compression and achieves up to 4.3 times end-to-end speedup on slower networks without sacrificing model quality. Combining it with gradient compression compresses all inter-machine communication and raises the reported maximum speedup to 4.9 times. These results connect a convergence argument to practical communication savings in the evaluated fine-tuning settings.
neurips-2022-fine-tuning-language-models.tldr: AQ-SGD compresses activation changes to accelerate pipeline-parallel language-model fine-tuning while providing a non-convex convergence guarantee.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics is used for sampling and for non-convex optimization. Variance-reduced versions aim to control variability in stochastic gradient estimates. This paper studies two such methods: Stochastic Variance Reduced Gradient Langevin Dynamics and Stochastic Recursive Gradient Langevin Dynamics, with the goal of strengthening their convergence analysis.

The authors prove convergence to the target distribution measured by KL-divergence. Their assumptions are smoothness and a Log-Sobolev inequality, which they describe as weaker than those used in earlier analyses of these algorithms. The contribution therefore concerns both the quality of the convergence bound and the conditions under which it holds.

With batch size and inner-loop length both set to the square root of n, the paper gives an improved gradient-complexity bound for reaching a specified precision. Its dependence includes a term proportional to n and another proportional to d times the square root of n divided by the target precision, alongside the stated problem factors and suppressed logarithms. The authors also develop applications of this sampling result to non-convex optimization.
neurips-2022-improved-convergence-rate-o.tldr: Two variance-reduced Langevin methods receive improved sampling convergence bounds under smoothness and a Log-Sobolev inequality.

paragraphs: Discovering causal relationships becomes difficult as the number of observed variables grows, because the space of possible graphs is combinatorial. This paper targets high-dimensional intervention datasets by introducing factor directed acyclic graphs. These graphs restrict the search to nonlinear, low-rank causal interaction models, providing a structural route to handling thousands of variables.

The authors combine this restriction with continuous optimization in an implementation called DCD-FG. It uses a Gaussian nonlinear low-rank structural equation model for interventional data. They also study random perturbations of graph edges as a model of statistical noise, quantifying how those perturbations affect factor-graph rank.

The theoretical analysis suggests that the restricted candidate space may be useful when high dimensionality makes the underlying graph skeleton difficult to estimate. Experiments show significant improvements over compared state-of-the-art methods in simulations and a large single-cell RNA sequencing dataset with hundreds of genetic interventions. The scalability result is linked to the low-rank modeling assumption: a more structured search space makes larger causal discovery problems tractable.
neurips-2022-large-scale-differentiable-.tldr: DCD-FG uses nonlinear low-rank factor graphs and continuous optimization to scale causal discovery to thousands of variables.

paragraphs: Sparse training reduces the number of active model weights, making it attractive for resource-limited devices. However, pushing sparsity to extreme levels can severely damage accuracy. This paper investigates two additional ways to reduce training costs so that efficiency improvements need not come entirely from removing more weights.

The first technique is layer freezing, which stops updating selected layers. Although used in dense training and fine-tuning, its compatibility with sparse training needs investigation because sparse models have distinct training characteristics. The second technique is data sieving, which reduces the training data used so that only part of the dataset participates throughout the training process.

The authors combine weight sparsity, layer freezing, and data sieving in a framework called SpFDE. Their analysis finds potential for substantial savings from freezing, and extensive experiments show that the combined framework can significantly reduce training costs while preserving accuracy. The contribution broadens sparse-training efficiency from a question about weight count to one that also considers which layers and examples require computation.
neurips-2022-layer-freezing-data-sieving.tldr: SpFDE combines sparse weights, layer freezing, and data sieving to reduce training costs while preserving accuracy in experiments.

paragraphs: Communication compression reduces the cost of exchanging information in distributed learning, but convergence guarantees alone do not establish how close an algorithm is to the best achievable performance. This paper supplies lower bounds for compressed distributed optimization in the smooth, non-convex stochastic setting, providing a reference against which algorithmic guarantees can be assessed.

The analysis covers compressors with either an unbiased or a contractive property. It also treats both worker-to-server compression and compression in both communication directions. By considering these combinations within the same study, the authors compare fundamental convergence limits across different ways of reducing communication.

The proposed algorithm, NEOLITHIC, approaches the lower bound up to a logarithmic factor under mild conditions. The results also show that bidirectional contractive compression can yield iterative methods converging as fast as methods using unbiased compression only from workers to the server. Experiments support the theoretical findings. The main contribution is a combination of performance limits and an algorithm that nearly attains them, with the stated conditions and logarithmic gap retained.
neurips-2022-lower-bounds-and-nearly-opt.tldr: The paper establishes compressed distributed-learning lower bounds and introduces NEOLITHIC, which nearly matches them under mild conditions.

paragraphs: Convenient implementations of machine-learning algorithms can consume too much memory to run on large problems. Making them fit often requires complicated programming outside the main computational framework. This paper addresses that burden at the compiler level, aiming to make memory-intensive methods usable without requiring developers to manage all memory-saving logic themselves.

The authors extend the XLA compiler so that it adjusts an algorithm's computational data-flow representation according to a memory limit supplied by the user. This places the memory constraint inside the process that transforms the computation for execution. The approach connects an explicit resource budget to how the algorithm's computation is organized.

The paper demonstrates larger single-device computations for k-nearest neighbors, sparse Gaussian process regression, and Transformers in cases where standard implementations fail. These examples support improved use of available hardware resources across several kinds of methods. The authors further suggest that compiler-level work on memory constraints could expand the range of machine-learning algorithms that researchers can develop and use.
neurips-2022-memory-safe-computations-wi.tldr: An XLA compiler extension reorganizes computations around a user-specified memory limit, enabling larger single-device workloads.

paragraphs: Bandits with knapsacks combines learning which actions earn rewards with constraints on resource use. In the standard formulation, each action consumes nonnegative amounts of resources, so budgets only decline. This paper generalizes the stochastic problem to allow resources to increase, decrease, or remain unchanged after an action.

The new formulation represents each outcome using a reward and resource drifts, which are added to the available budgets. The authors first consider a decision-maker who knows the true outcome distributions. For that setting, they construct a Markov decision process policy with constant regret relative to a linear programming relaxation.

They then use this result to build an algorithm for unknown outcome distributions, obtaining logarithmic regret against the same relaxation. The comparison target matters: the guarantees are explicitly measured against that linear programming benchmark. A reduction from ordinary bandits with knapsacks shows that the regret bound matches existing results. The work extends resource-constrained learning to replenishable resources while connecting its guarantees to the established consumption-only setting.
neurips-2022-non-monotonic-resource-util.tldr: A bandit model allowing resource replenishment admits logarithmic learning regret against a linear programming relaxation.

paragraphs: When several objectives compete, optimization aims to identify useful tradeoffs rather than a single universally best solution. Expensive evaluations make this especially challenging. Existing multi-objective Bayesian optimization methods typically return a finite collection of solutions, which may omit the tradeoff a decision-maker would most prefer.

This paper proposes learning a model that approximates the whole Pareto set. The approach generalizes decomposition-based multi-objective optimization from a finite population of candidates to a model of the solution set. It uses that learned structure to design an acquisition search method for selecting evaluations, with natural support for evaluating batches.

The learned approximation also lets decision-makers explore different tradeoff regions instead of choosing only among a fixed list of evaluated candidates. Experiments on synthetic and real-world problems demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The contribution is an approach to representing and searching a continuous family of tradeoffs under a limited evaluation budget; the learned set remains an approximation, rather than an exact recovery of every Pareto-optimal solution.
neurips-2022-pareto-set-learning-for-exp.tldr: Learning an approximate Pareto set helps guide expensive evaluations and lets users explore a continuous range of objective tradeoffs.

paragraphs: Traffic forecasting models learn dependencies across locations and time, but their predictions can become vulnerable when incoming data are manipulated. This paper studies that vulnerability under an attack framework that selects particular data-source nodes rather than requiring simultaneous access to every geographically distributed source.

The framework has two stages. An iterative gradient-guided saliency method identifies victim nodes whose selection can change over time. A spatiotemporal gradient-based procedure then constructs real-valued adversarial traffic states subject to a perturbation constraint. The authors also provide a theoretical bound on worst-case forecasting performance under adversarial attacks.

Experiments on two real-world datasets report up to 67.8% performance degradation across advanced spatiotemporal forecasting models. This is a maximum observed degradation, not a uniform effect across all models or conditions. The authors additionally show that adversarial training with these attacks can significantly improve robustness. The study therefore supplies evidence of vulnerability and a way to use the identified attacks during training to strengthen the evaluated forecasting models.
neurips-2022-practical-adversarial-attac.tldr: Targeted perturbations of selected traffic-data nodes substantially degrade forecasts in experiments and can support robustness-improving adversarial training.

paragraphs: Backdoor attacks tamper with training data so that a model later exhibits a vulnerability when a trigger appears in its input. Conventional attacks place the trigger directly in training examples, where inspection may reveal it. Hidden-trigger attacks seek to create the vulnerability without putting that trigger into the training data.

The paper addresses a weakness of an existing hidden-trigger approach: it does not effectively poison networks trained from scratch. The proposed attack, Sleeper Agent, combines gradient matching, data selection, and retraining of the target model during the crafting process. These components are used together to create poisoned data that affect the eventual trained network.

The authors report that Sleeper Agent is the first effective hidden-trigger backdoor attack against networks trained from scratch. They demonstrate effectiveness on ImageNet and in black-box settings. The finding expands the demonstrated reach of hidden-trigger poisoning: the absence of the eventual trigger from training examples does not prevent such a vulnerability from being learned in the settings evaluated.
neurips-2022-sleeper-agent-scalable-hidd.tldr: Sleeper Agent demonstrates hidden-trigger backdoor poisoning against neural networks trained from scratch, including ImageNet and black-box settings.

paragraphs: Neural-network initialization is often chosen using handcrafted rules tied to particular architectures. This paper explores automating that choice. It introduces GradCosine, a differentiable measure of how closely gradients from individual training samples point in the same direction at the initialized parameters.

The authors analyze the optimization landscape at the sample level and show that maximizing GradCosine under a gradient-norm constraint can improve training and test performance. The norm constraint is part of the stated result. They turn this observation into neural initialization optimization, or NIO, extending the analysis into a practical batch-based procedure for finding a better starting point.

The paper reports that NIO adds negligible cost relative to training time and improves classification performance across several architectures on CIFAR10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet. It also finds that the method can help train a large vision Transformer without warmup. These results support using gradient agreement to guide initialization, while the warmup finding remains an observed capability rather than a universal replacement for warmup.
neurips-2022-towards-theoretically-inspi.tldr: NIO automatically improves initialization by promoting sample-gradient alignment under a gradient-norm constraint, with classification gains in experiments.

paragraphs: Monte Carlo integration supports randomized approximation methods and can distribute work across many computing resources. Delegation introduces a verification problem when some computations contain accidental or adversarial errors. This paper asks how to accompany the result with evidence of correctness that is cheaper to check than recomputing the answer.

The authors organize the computations around an algebraic proof system from computational complexity theory. The proof is represented by a polynomial, and evaluating it at a randomly chosen point verifies it with probabilistic guarantees. This shifts the task from repeating the entire computation to checking a mathematical certificate.

They give verifiable extensions of known Monte Carlo estimators for zero-one matrix permanents, model counts of disjunctive normal form formulas, and logistic-regression gradients. These extensions have moderate computational overhead, while verification requires substantially fewer resources than starting over with state-of-the-art algorithms. The paper also discusses challenges in engineering broader verifiable approximation schemes. Its contribution is probabilistic verification of delegated approximation computations, with concrete examples demonstrating the approach.
neurips-2022-trustworthy-monte-carlo-c08.tldr: Algebraic proof systems let selected Monte Carlo computations carry correctness evidence that is cheaper to verify than to recompute.

paragraphs: Model-based offline reinforcement learning relies on a learned dynamics model while using previously collected data. Uncertainty estimates help assess model error, which matters when the learned model encounters examples outside the data distribution. This paper proposes combining parametric and nonparametric uncertainty methods through a metric defined in latent space.

The metric uses Riemannian geometry associated with an encoder-decoder forward model. Specifically, the authors construct a pullback metric, tying the latent-space measurement to the learned model. Their proposed measure captures both the quality of out-of-distribution samples and discrepancies among examples in the data, bringing these two sources of information into one uncertainty estimate.

They integrate the combined estimate into a pessimistic model-based reinforcement-learning framework, where uncertainty informs cautious treatment of model predictions. Experiments on continuous-control and autonomous-driving benchmarks show significant improvements over contemporary model-based offline approaches. The findings support using model-informed latent geometry for uncertainty estimation in the evaluated settings, connecting a geometric construction to the practical quality of learned decision-making.
neurips-2022-uncertainty-estimation-usin.tldr: A geometry-based latent metric combines uncertainty estimates and improves pessimistic model-based offline reinforcement learning on evaluated benchmarks.
